sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Appointment Year & Context**: Appointed in **1886** by Lord Dufferin to address Indian demands for greater representation in the civil service following the lowering of the age limit for the ICS exam to 19 years in 1876 under Lord Lytton.
• **Abolition of Statutory Civil Service**: The committee recommended the abolition of the **Statutory Civil Service** established in 1879, which had proven to be a failure in satisfying Indian aspirations.
• **Service Restructuring**: Proposed a three-tier classification system consisting of **Imperial Civil Service** (recruited in London), **Provincial Civil Service** (recruited in India), and **Subordinate Civil Service** (recruited locally).
• **Age Limit Adjustment**: Recommended raising the maximum age limit for the civil service examination to **23 years** to give fair chances to Indian candidates.

items.definition: The elite cadre of the civil service whose members signed covenants with the East India Company/Crown; later transformed into the Indian Civil Service (ICS).
A diverse category of lower and middle government posts held largely by Indians, which the Aitchison Committee reorganized into Provincial and Subordinate services.
A short-lived scheme (1879) allowing provincial governments to appoint Indians of high families to a fraction of ICS posts; criticized as aristocratic patronage and abolished by Aitchison.
The core demand of Indian nationalists (like the Indian National Congress) for holding ICS exams concurrently in England and India—a demand explicitly rejected by the Aitchison Committee.

items.title: Major Geographical Distribution / Regional Hubs
items.content:
• **Imperial Hub**: London, United Kingdom (sole venue for Imperial Civil Service examinations, favoring British candidates with financial means and access to Western education).
• **Provincial Hubs**: Presidency capitals (Calcutta, Bombay, Madras) and major provincial headquarters where Provincial Civil Services were examined and posted.

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Bottlenecks / Issues**: Continued racial exclusion at the top executive tier, rejection of simultaneous exams, and creation of lower-status provincial cadres.
• **Policy Interventions**: Led to subsequent public service commissions, notably the **Islington Commission (1912)** and the **Lee Commission (1924)** which eventually paved the way for more substantive Indianization.

items.title: Mnemonic for Civil Service Classifications under Aitchison
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: "IPS" (Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate)
• **Decoded Meaning**: Imperial (Top/London), Provincial (Middle/Local), Subordinate (Base/Clerical).
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Quickly identifies structural tiers recommended in 1886 without confusing them with later commission structures.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Aitchison = 1886 = Abolished Statutory Service = Rejected Simultaneous Exams = Introduced Provincial Service.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often frames statements claiming the Aitchison Committee recommended holding simultaneous civil service exams in India and England. This is false; the committee explicitly rejected simultaneous examinations.

Mains Value Addition: Use the Aitchison Committee to illustrate the 'safety valve' or limited concession strategy of British colonial administration—offering lower-tier provincial posts while guarding the imperial steel frame.

keyTakeaways: The Aitchison Committee (1886) recommended abolishing the unsuccessful Statutory Civil Service.
It restructured services into Imperial, Provincial, and Subordinate tiers, formally categorizing administrative roles.
It notoriously rejected the Indian National Congress demand for simultaneous competitive examinations in India and England.
